subject: obstetrics-gynaecology
title: Uterine Artery and Ureter, Ovarian Drainage and Pelvic Floor

steps.tx: The ureter passes beneath the uterine artery near the cervix, remembered as water under the bridge, the **uterine artery ureter relation**. It is the commonest site of ureteric injury in hysterectomy. Identifying the ureter before clamping the artery prevents it. The ureter lies about 1.5 to 2 centimetres lateral to the cervix where the artery crosses above it.
steps.say: The ureter passes under the uterine artery, the commonest hysterectomy injury site.

steps.tx: Ovarian lymph drains along the ovarian vessels to para aortic nodes at renal level, termed **ovarian lymphatic drainage**. This is why ovarian cancer staging samples high para aortic nodes. Uterine drainage goes instead to pelvic node groups. Fundus drainage also reaches para aortic nodes through this route, a second path examiners ask about.
steps.say: Ovarian lymphatic drainage reaches para aortic nodes at renal level along its vessels.

steps.tx: The muscular and fascial diaphragm closing the pelvic outlet is the **pelvic floor**. Levator ani and coccygeus with their fascia support bladder, uterus and rectum against abdominal pressure. Childbirth injury here is the root of later prolapse. Level three support is the perineal membrane and perineal body anchoring the lower vagina.
steps.say: The pelvic floor diaphragm supports pelvic organs against abdominal pressure.

vis.alt: Superior and coronal views of the female pelvic diaphragm showing levator ani and coccygeus pierced by urethra, vagina, and anal canal.
vis.caption: Superior and coronal views of the female pelvic diaphragm showing levator ani (puborectalis, pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus) and coccygeus pierced by urethra, vagina, and anal canal. Pelvic diaphragm (levator ani and coccygeus) and pelvic floor hiatuses.

steps.tx: The uterine artery arises from the internal iliac and reaches the uterus at internal os level, called the **uterine artery course**. It anastomoses freely with ovarian and vaginal branches. This collateral web explains pelvic embolisation safety. The artery crosses the ureter anteriorly from lateral to medial just above the lateral vaginal fornix.
steps.say: The uterine artery course anastomoses with ovarian and vaginal branches freely.

steps.tx: The ureter enters the pelvis crossing the common iliac bifurcation, a landmark of the **pelvic ureter course**. It then runs medial to the internal iliac under the uterine artery tunnel. Surgeons recite this course before every pelvic operation. It also passes medial to the internal iliac artery branches and lateral to the cardinal ligament tunnel.
steps.say: The pelvic ureter crosses the iliac bifurcation then passes under the uterine artery.

steps.tx: Ovarian vessels travel in the suspensory ligament and anastomose at the cornu, forming the **ovarian vascular pedicle**. Unrecognised bleeding here retracts into the retroperitoneum silently. Methodical pedicle control prevents broad ligament haematomas. A broad ligament haematoma can hide a litre of blood while the abdomen still looks flat.
steps.say: The ovarian vascular pedicle retracts and bleeds retroperitoneally if uncontrolled.

steps.tx: Supports of the uterus rank from levator tone to cardinal and uterosacral ligaments as the **three tier support** system. DeLancey levels describe apical, mid vaginal and distal support for prolapse surgery. Failure at each level produces distinct prolapses. DeLancey level one failure gives vault or uterine prolapse; level two gives anterior and posterior wall prolapse.
steps.say: Three tier support by DeLancey levels explains distinct prolapse types by failure level.

steps.tx: The pudendal nerve through Alcock canal supplies the perineum and is blocked for outlet procedures by the **pudendal block**. Bilateral transvaginal injection at the ischial spine anaesthetises the lower vagina. It serves forceps deliveries and perineal repair. Ten millilitres of local anaesthetic each side is the standard pudendal block volume.
steps.say: Pudendal block at the ischial spine anaesthetises the perineum for outlet procedures.

steps.tx: The ureter is injured by surgeons who forget where it travels, not by bad luck. **Ureter protection strategies** include identifying it at the pelvic brim, keeping clamps close to the uterus, using lighted stents or dyes in hostile pelves, and checking efflux when injury is suspected. Water under the bridge is the aide memoire at hysterectomy, where the uterine artery crosses above it. Deliberate identification beats cautious avoidance in a scarred operative field.
steps.say: Protecting the ureter means identifying it deliberately, clamping close to the uterus and checking when in doubt. Identification beats avoidance in scarred fields.

vis.alt: Image showing ureter protection strategies during pelvic surgery near the uterine artery.
vis.caption: The ureter is shown identified and protected where the uterine artery crosses above it. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Preserving ureteric safety uses visualisation, palpation of vermiculation and sometimes stents, grouped as **ureter protection strategies**. Lighted stents and fluorescence imaging are modern adjuncts in difficult cases. None replaces knowing the anatomy cold. Preoperative stents make the ureter palpable as a cord that snaps, a trick senior surgeons still teach.
steps.say: Ureter protection strategies assist but never replace knowing the anatomy cold.
